paraphrase: Thesis, decided by the six marks. The text presents Bhairava's supreme state, which is also the Goddess Parā, as unspeakable fullness, free of direction, time and place and not any of the forms with parts (vv.7-21), and offers, as the means of entering it, a run of short contemplations of the waveless state (24-138), each turning the mind to something in ordinary experience (a breath, a void, a sound's end, the middle between two states, joy, the thought that all is consciousness) or away from the mind's supports; established in any one of them one becomes Bhairava (140), and the outer acts of worship are to be understood as these inner acts (144-153). Marks. Opening and closing (upakrama/upasaṃhāra): opens with the Goddess's question about Bhairava's form (1-6) and closes with her statement that the essence of the Rudrayāmala has been ascertained (161-162). Repetition (abhyāsa): the refrains of the thought-free (nirvikalpa), the supportless (nirādhāra), the void (śūnya), 'made of it' (tanmaya), endings on 'Bhairava's form' (84, 112, 138) and 'wherever the mind goes' (116, 129). Novelty (apūrvatā): 'the essence of tantra, most secret' (7-8, 157). Stated result (phala): 140-142 and 148, and a result at the end of most verses. Praise (arthavāda): 141, 156 ('easy'), 157-160. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): 5-6 (supremacy is contradicted by having parts), 18-19 (power and fire), 110 (waves and water), 134-137, 152-153.
